strengths: Significance: DMPO addresses an important problem: adapting reinforcement learning to masked diffusion LLMs without repeatedly estimating current-policy sequence likelihoods. Reusing clean rollouts through a weighted denoising objective is a useful practical direction.

Empirical results: Table 1 shows substantial improvements on planning tasks. At generation length 256, Countdown accuracy increases from 26.56% for d1 to 75.78%, and Sudoku from 11.04% to 24.56%. Improvements generally persist across three generation lengths, although gains on mathematical reasoning are smaller.

Originality: Adapting distribution matching to dLLM reasoning and investigating negative-weight corrections provides a potentially useful contribution. The paper appropriately credits MDNS for weighted denoising cross-entropy and prior work for direct discriminative optimization.

Presentation and transparency: The manuscript has a clear overall structure, explicit objectives, and useful algorithmic illustrations. Appendix C provides rewards and many training settings. The authors acknowledge the single-backbone scope and report WDDO instability rather than concealing it. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central guarantees do not extend to the implemented method. Equation (11) replaces sequence cross-entropy with a denoising upper bound; subsequent baseline subtraction introduces signed weights. The manuscript does not establish that these modifications preserve the target distribution or provide the claimed convergence guarantees. Appendix B.2 explicitly acknowledges that the score-function argument only applies approximately after replacing log likelihood with the ELBO, but does not bound this approximation. More seriously, the individual baseline subtracts an expectation under a different, negatively tilted distribution. Even with exact likelihoods, this generally changes the optimum and can make the signed cross-entropy objective unbounded below. This matters because Section 4 attributes the strongest Countdown results to that baseline.

Soundness and reproducibility—weight normalization is inconsistent. Section 3.2 specifies softmax-normalized weights, which sum to one, while Equation (13) subtracts one from every weight and Equations (14)–(15) use baselines summing to N. Taken literally, the group-baseline version assigns negative weights to every response for N > 1. Presumably the positive weights should also be multiplied by N, but that essential scaling is not specified. This changes update directions, not merely the learning rate.

Reproducibility: Appendix C omits the reward temperature alpha and buffer-refresh frequency F, both central algorithmic parameters. It also does not adequately specify how reference-policy likelihoods and importance ratios are obtained under the actual blockwise sampler. Section 4 says Countdown uses the individual baseline, whereas Appendix C.2 says Table 1 uses the group baseline. These omissions and contradictions prevent an unambiguous reconstruction of the reported method.

Evidence for the proposed mechanism is insufficient. The paper motivates distribution matching through diversity preservation, mode coverage, and reduced reward hacking, but measures accuracy and training reward without evaluating those properties. Figure 5 supports the usefulness of baseline subtraction on Sudoku, but a single rollout-group size does not establish the claimed small-batch failure mechanism. Batch-size sweeps and a tractable distribution-matching experiment would help distinguish principled target matching from heuristic reward-weighted optimization.

Evaluation limits confidence in broader superiority. Only d1 is directly compared as an RL training algorithm, despite discussion of other relevant approaches. There are no repeated training runs or uncertainty estimates, making the modest GSM8K and MATH500 gains difficult to assess. The 256-example synthetic evaluations lack sufficient generation and overlap-checking details. Checkpoint-selection procedures and baseline-selection criteria are also unclear.

Efficiency and presentation claims exceed the evidence. There are no wall-clock, memory, likelihood-estimation-cost, or replay-frequency comparisons supporting the proposed efficiency advantages; evaluation uses one denoising step per generated token. Appendix B.1 acknowledges that eliminating reference likelihood ratios requires a different zero-temperature formulation. The headline 42.9% and 55.8% improvements are average percentage-point gains on Countdown, rather than relative percentage improvements. The promising empirical gains do not outweigh the unresolved objective and reproducibility issues.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful problem: reinforcement learning for masked diffusion language models without repeatedly evaluating the current policy's full rollout likelihood. Reusing clean responses through weighted denoising is an appealing approach.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports substantial planning-task improvements. At length 256, Countdown accuracy increases from 26.56% for d1 to 75.78%, and Sudoku from 11.04% to 24.56%. These gains warrant further investigation, even though improvements on mathematical reasoning are smaller.

Originality: Adapting distribution matching to dLLM reasoning and investigating negative-weight corrections provides a potentially useful contribution. Figure 5 offers evidence that baseline subtraction materially affects training.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally readable and includes pseudocode, reward definitions, optimizer settings, adaptation settings, and decoding details. It appropriately acknowledges the single-backbone evaluation and reports WDDO instability. I identified no material research-ethics concern in the described work.
weaknesses: Soundness—central guarantee does not extend to the successful algorithm: The distribution-matching argument concerns positive-weight WDCE, whereas the reported improvements depend on subtracting baselines. In particular, the individual baseline in Eq. (14) subtracts a negative-reward target distribution. Even with exact likelihoods, this produces a difference of cross-entropies whose optimum generally is not p*. Negative coefficients can make that objective unbounded below. Appendix B.2 gives only an approximate variance-reduction argument for the other baselines and acknowledges that replacing log likelihood with the ELBO breaks the exact identity. The manuscript therefore does not establish that its implemented updates preserve the claimed target distribution.

Soundness—order-dependent distributions require correction: Eq. (8) uses the order-averaged partition function Z(q) to define an order-specific conditional distribution. Generally, its total mass is Z_sigma(q)/Z(q), rather than one. Eq. (9) can be interpreted using an unnormalized joint measure, but the claim that every normalized order-specific policy can match Eq. (8) does not follow. Furthermore, the uniform-permutation formulation is not reconciled with the blockwise semi-autoregressive sampler used in Appendix C.2. These gaps matter for the importance-weight interpretation.

Evidence does not establish the proposed mechanism: Evaluation measures accuracy and training rewards, but not response diversity, mode coverage, distance to the target distribution, or resistance to reward hacking. Thus, the principal motivation for forward KL remains untested. Figure 5 studies baseline choices on one task at one rollout count; it does not isolate small batch size as the cause of vanilla WDCE's failure.

Reproducibility has consequential omissions and inconsistencies: Appendix C.2 does not specify the reward temperature alpha or buffer refresh frequency F, and does not adequately explain how the required reference-policy trajectory likelihoods are computed. Section 4 says Countdown uses the individual baseline, while Appendix C.2 says Table 1 uses the group baseline. Section 3.2 describes ordinary softmax weights, whereas Eqs. (13)–(15) require weights scaled to have mean one. These choices materially change the update.

Evaluation protocol needs clarification: Appendix C.1 refers to a MATH500 training split without identifying the actual training corpus and its separation from evaluation. Synthetic Countdown and Sudoku evaluation sets lack seeds and explicit train–test overlap checks. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, limiting confidence in the smaller mathematical-reasoning gains. The Sudoku accuracy metric also needs an explicit definition distinguishing complete-puzzle success from cell-level correctness.

Comparative significance and efficiency remain incompletely supported: d1 is the only directly evaluated RL algorithm, despite discussion of other relevant methods. Training budgets differ, and no wall-clock, memory, or sample-efficiency measurements substantiate the efficiency claims. Appendix B.1 itself notes that eliminating likelihood-ratio computation entirely requires a special zero-regularization variant, whose diversity guarantee is relinquished.

Originality and presentation claims are overstated: WDCE is explicitly inherited from MDNS, and WDDO adapts an existing discriminative objective, so the novel contribution should be delineated more narrowly. Statements of consistent superiority overlook GSM8K at length 128, where d1 performs better, and MATH500 at length 128, where Dream performs better. The headline 42.9% and 55.8% gains are average percentage-point differences, not relative percentage improvements. Overall, the promising empirical contribution does not compensate for unresolved central theoretical and reproducibility issues.

strengths: Significance: Table 1 reports substantial improvements on planning tasks. At generation length 256, DMPO achieves 75.78% on Countdown versus 26.56% for d1, and 24.56% on Sudoku versus 11.04%. These are useful empirical results that merit further investigation.

Soundness: The idealized forward-KL formulation provides a reasonable foundation for reward-weighted denoising training. Appendix B.3 establishes the optimum of the exact DDO objective, and Figure 5 provides evidence that negative-gradient insertion matters in the tested Sudoku setting.

Originality: Adapting distribution matching to diffusion-language-model reasoning, with reusable rollouts and several weight-baseline choices, is a useful methodological contribution. The manuscript appropriately credits MDNS for WDCE and prior work for the discriminative objective.

Presentation and limitations: The main framework is clearly organized, and the appendix supplies reward definitions, optimizer settings, and decoding details. The authors candidly acknowledge evaluation on one backbone and four elementary benchmarks and report WDDO instability. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central guarantees do not extend to the practical objective. Appendix B.2 correctly acknowledges that baseline subtraction is only approximate variance reduction after replacing log likelihood with the denoising ELBO, but does not bound the resulting bias or establish the claimed target as a fixed point. More seriously, the individual baseline in Eq. (14) subtracts expectations under a distinct negative-reward distribution. Even with exact likelihoods, this generally changes the optimum; the resulting signed cross-entropy can be unbounded below. This variant produces the headline Countdown results, so its connection to distribution matching requires justification.

Soundness—the order-dependent formulation needs correction and reconciliation with implementation. In Eq. (8), dividing each order-specific tilted distribution by the shared Z(q) does not generally normalize it for each order. The mixture identity can still hold using unnormalized measures, but the stated conditional-distribution interpretation is incorrect without an additional assumption. Furthermore, the derivation averages uniformly over all token permutations, whereas Appendix C.2 uses blockwise semi-autoregressive sampling. The manuscript does not explain how its target and importance weights account for this change.

Evidence does not establish the central diversity and efficiency claims. There are no measurements of reasoning-path diversity, mode coverage, reward hacking, or distance to the target distribution. Greedy benchmark accuracy cannot validate these properties. Likewise, no wall-clock, memory, effective-sample-size, or replay-frequency comparisons substantiate improved training efficiency or sample efficiency. Computing the reference-policy likelihood ratios remains a relevant cost.

Evaluation is insufficient to establish broad superiority. d1 is the only trained RL comparator, although the related-work discussion identifies several relevant alternatives. The comparison also changes the SFT recipe and training schedule without isolating their effects. There are no repeated training seeds or uncertainty estimates; this particularly limits interpretation of the smaller GSM8K and MATH500 gains. Figure 5 studies one task at one rollout count, so it does not establish that the observed failure specifically arises from small batches.

Reproducibility has material gaps. The reward temperature alpha and buffer refresh frequency F are not specified. Section 3.2 describes softmax-normalized weights, while subtracting 1 in Eq. (13) appears to require weights scaled to mean one. Section 4 says Countdown uses the individual baseline, whereas Appendix C.2 says the main results use the group baseline. Dataset partition sizes, synthetic evaluation seeds, and overlap checks also need clarification, particularly the stated MATH500 training split.

Presentation overstates the results: claims of consistent superiority conflict with Table 1, where DMPO trails d1 on GSM8K at length 128 and Dream on MATH500 at length 128. More broadly, theoretical guarantees should be distinguished from heuristic approximations and empirical improvements. The promising planning results do not resolve the central soundness and reproducibility issues, which prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Significance: Reusing generated responses through weighted denoising is a useful direction for diffusion-LLM post-training. Table 1 reports substantial Countdown improvements: at length 256, DMPO-LLaDA reaches 80.86 versus 42.58 for cGRPO and 26.56 for d1. These gains warrant further investigation.

Experimental merits: The paper evaluates four tasks, three generation lengths, and several LLaDA starting checkpoints. Ablations examine baseline subtraction, rollout count, buffer reuse, and fast sampling. Figure 4 provides useful evidence that negative gradients are essential to the practical method.

Originality: Although distribution matching, WDCE, and discriminative objectives build on acknowledged prior work, adapting them to diffusion-LLM reasoning and investigating weight baselines offers a potentially useful methodological contribution.

Presentation and limitations: The main exposition clearly motivates the approach and distinguishes its components. The appendix provides rewards, optimizer settings, and decoding configurations. The conclusion appropriately acknowledges the restricted model and task coverage; no material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—baseline subtraction undermines the central guarantee. The individual baseline in Eq. (14) subtracts an expectation under a negative-reward target distribution. This generally changes the population objective: even with exact sequence likelihoods, p_theta = p* need not be stationary, and the resulting signed cross-entropy can be unbounded below. Appendix B.3 only motivates approximate gradient preservation for the group/model baselines, not the individual baseline. This matters directly because Appendix C.2 uses the individual baseline for the strongest Countdown result and all SFT/1.5 variants. Their performance therefore does not establish the claimed matching of the reward-tilted distribution.

Soundness—the path-space justification requires correction. Equation (8) uses a common Z(q), although the reward normalizer can depend on generation order; these order-specific quantities need not individually be probability distributions. A joint importance-sampling derivation can repair this notation, but Appendix B.1 has a deeper gap: Eq. (21) retains the reference trajectory conditional on the endpoint, whereas randomly remasking endpoints constructs a different path distribution in general. Consequently, the subsequent equality KL(P* || P_theta) + const = E_p*[L_theta] requires additional consistency assumptions. WDCE remains a plausible surrogate, but the claimed exact SOC equivalence is not established.

Soundness and implementation: The importance ratios are derived for categorical random-order sampling, whereas Appendix C.2 uses semi-autoregressive greedy sampling and temperature-0.2 fast-dLLM sampling. The manuscript does not explain how the denominator probabilities account for these sampling distributions, restricted support, or heuristic unmasking. Independence of weights from the current parameters does not by itself make these ratios correct or ensure low variance. This gap affects both the distribution-matching and efficiency claims.

Reproducibility: Essential settings are missing or inconsistent. The reward temperature alpha and default buffer frequency for Table 1 are not specified. Section 3.2 describes softmax-normalized weights, while Eqs. (13)–(15) imply weights normalized to mean one; the required scaling is not explicit. Appendix C.2 first specifies task-dependent baselines, then states that Table 1 uses the group baseline. The actual likelihood-ratio estimator and its computational cost also need clarification. No implementation link is provided.

Experimental support: Table 1 lacks repeated-run variability or confidence intervals, making the smaller math and Sudoku differences difficult to interpret. Countdown and Sudoku use only 256 evaluation instances, and train/test overlap checks for the synthetic puzzles are not reported. Figure 9 measures predictive token entropy along sampled trajectories, which does not establish coverage of distinct successful reasoning modes or reduced reward hacking. Those central distributional claims need direct evaluation.

Presentation and claim calibration: The claim of consistently outperforming d1/cGRPO has exceptions, including DMPO-LLaDA on GSM8K at length 128 and Sudoku at length 512. The headline gains also conflate percentage-point differences with percentage improvements. Overall, the promising empirical contribution does not compensate for unresolved mathematical and implementation gaps in the paper's central guarantees.

strengths: Significance: Efficient RL post-training for diffusion LLMs is a useful problem. Reusing rollouts with a weighted denoising objective is practically attractive, and Table 1 reports substantial Countdown improvements: DMPO-LLaDA reaches 80.86% versus 42.58% for cGRPO at length 256.

Soundness: The idealized reward-tilted target and importance-weighted denoising construction provide a reasonable starting point. The exact-likelihood WDDO objective has a clear minimizer argument in Appendix B.4.

Evaluation: The paper examines four tasks, three generation lengths, alternative weight baselines, buffer reuse, rollout counts, and accelerated sampling. Figure 4 usefully demonstrates that baseline subtraction is essential to the reported training behavior.

Presentation and limitations: The main algorithmic motivation is accessible, and the appendix supplies rewards, several training settings, and additional experiments. The conclusion appropriately acknowledges the limited model and task coverage. I found no material research-ethics concern in the described application.
weaknesses: Soundness—central guarantees do not extend to the successful algorithm. The individual baseline in Eq. (14) subtracts an expectation under a different, negatively reward-tilted distribution; this changes the objective rather than merely reducing variance. Even with exact likelihoods, the resulting signed cross-entropy need not be minimized at p*, and can be unbounded below. This matters because Appendix C.2 assigns this baseline to the strongest Countdown result. The group baseline is also only approximately gradient-preserving with stale rollouts and an ELBO surrogate, as Appendix B.3 acknowledges. No analysis establishes distribution matching for these implemented variants.

Soundness—the importance-sampling assumptions differ materially from actual generation. Equations (1) and (10) use uniformly random-order categorical sampling, whereas Appendix C.2 uses blockwise generation at temperature zero or confidence-based Fast-dLLM at temperature 0.2. These induce different proposal distributions; greedy sampling also removes support required by the stated correction. The manuscript does not explain how weights account for these differences or quantify the resulting bias.

Theory: Eq. (8) generally does not define a normalized order-conditional distribution: its normalizer can depend on the order, whereas Z(q) averages over orders. A joint importance-sampling formulation can repair this, but the stated interpretation needs correction. Appendix B.1 also equates denoising training with KL to the reward-tilted reference path measure, although random remasking constructs a different conditional path distribution unless additional consistency assumptions hold. Thus the claimed exact path-level justification is not established as written.

Reproducibility: The reward temperature alpha is not reported, and the main experiments' buffer frequency and sampler assignment are unclear. Section 3.2 describes softmax-normalized weights, but Eq. (13) subtracts 1 and Eqs. (14–15) use N-scaled softmax; the required scaling of the positive weights is unspecified. Appendix C.2 first assigns different baselines by task/model, then says Table 1 uses the group baseline throughout. These ambiguities prevent faithful reconstruction of the central method.

Evaluation reliability: Appendix C.1 describes training on a MATH500 training split without clearly identifying its construction or separation from evaluation. Synthetic Countdown and Sudoku evaluation sets lack seeds and documented overlap checks. Training-seed variation and confidence intervals are absent, limiting interpretation of the modest mathematics gains and results on only 256 planning examples. These are unresolved validation questions, not evidence that contamination occurred.

Significance and presentation: Claims of consistent superiority and preserved reasoning diversity exceed the evidence. DMPO-LLaDA trails d1 on GSM8K at length 128 and cGRPO on Sudoku at length 512. The headline 54.3 improvement matches the Countdown percentage-point gain over d1, rather than the stronger cGRPO comparator in that column. Figure 9 measures average predictive token entropy, which does not establish coverage of distinct correct reasoning paths or resistance to reward hacking.

Originality: The manuscript explicitly inherits WDCE from MDNS and adapts an existing discriminative objective. The potentially distinctive contribution is their effective adaptation through baseline subtraction and rollout reuse, but the theoretical gaps and implementation ambiguities prevent this contribution from being reliably established. The practical promise is insufficient to outweigh these issues.

strengths: Significance: Efficient reinforcement learning for diffusion LLMs is a useful problem. Reusing generated responses through weighted denoising offers a practical approach, and Figure 5 provides encouraging evidence of improved training efficiency on Countdown.

Empirical contribution: Table 1 shows substantial Countdown gains: at generation length 256, DMPO-LLaDA achieves 80.86 versus 42.58 for cGRPO and 26.56 for d1. Improvements also appear on mathematical reasoning tasks, although they are smaller.

Originality: The adaptation of distribution matching to diffusion-LM post-training, together with experiments on negative-weight baselines and replay reuse, constitutes a discernible contribution. Figures 4, 7, and 8 help identify which implementation choices matter.

Presentation and transparency: The manuscript is generally readable, supplies pseudocode and substantial experimental detail, and acknowledges its restriction to one model family and elementary reasoning tasks. That honest limitation discussion is appropriate. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described applications.
weaknesses: Soundness—baseline subtraction changes the central objective: The individual baseline in Equation (14) subtracts an expectation under a different, negatively reward-tilted distribution. Even with exact likelihoods and population expectations, this is not a zero-mean control variate: at p_theta = p*, its gradient generally remains nonzero. Thus the implemented objective need not match the claimed target distribution and can be unbounded below when coefficients are negative. This matters directly because Appendix C.2 assigns this baseline to Countdown, the strongest result, and to all SFT/1.5 variants. Appendix B.3 only motivates the group/model baselines approximately and does not resolve this issue.

Soundness—the importance-sampling derivation does not cover the actual rollout policies: Equations (1) and (10) require sampling from the stated stochastic, random-order policy and evaluating its probability ratio. Appendix C.2 instead reports temperature-zero semi-autoregressive sampling and temperature-0.2 Fast-dLLM with heuristic decoding. These procedures change the proposal distribution; greedy sampling can also remove required support. The paper does not explain the corresponding likelihood correction or quantify the resulting bias. Consequently, its exact distribution-matching and off-policy guarantees are not established for the experiments.

Soundness—the path-space justification needs correction: Equation (8) uses a common Z(q) for every order, although each order-specific reward-tilted measure need not normalize individually. A joint distribution over responses and orders can repair the importance-sampling formulation, but not the stated conditional interpretation. More materially, Appendix B.1 identifies the terminally tilted reference path measure in Equation (21) with the path measure obtained by uniformly masking samples from p*. These generally differ for an order-dependent reference model, so the asserted equality between path KL and expected denoising loss needs additional assumptions. The ordinary ELBO bound alone does not establish this equality.

Evaluation: Results lack repeated training runs or uncertainty estimates, while Countdown and Sudoku each use only 256 evaluation instances. Figure 9 measures average predictive token entropy along rollout contexts, which does not establish coverage of distinct successful reasoning paths or reduced reward hacking. The large Countdown improvement is promising, but the proposed explanation and smaller benchmark gains need stronger evidence.

Reproducibility: Appendix C.2 does not specify the reward-tilting temperature alpha, distinct from decoding temperature and LoRA scaling. Weight normalization is also ambiguous: ordinary softmax weights sum to one, whereas Equation (13) subtracts one and Equations (14)–(15) explicitly scale by N. The appendix additionally gives conflicting descriptions of which baselines produce Table 1. Exact training splits, generated evaluation sets/seeds, and sufficient cGRPO reproduction details are needed; the MATH500 'train split' description is particularly unclear.

Originality and claim calibration: WDCE and its importance-sampling construction are explicitly inherited from MDNS, and the reward-tilted optimum follows from the same regularized reward-maximization objective already presented in Equation (4). The novelty is therefore primarily the adaptation and training modifications, whose guarantees require the repairs above. Claims of consistent superiority are also too broad: DMPO-LLaDA loses to d1 on GSM8K at length 128 and to cGRPO on Sudoku at length 512. The headline 54.3% improvement is a percentage-point difference against d1, not the strongest listed Countdown baseline. These unresolved methodological and reproducibility issues outweigh the promising empirical contribution.
